chapter: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
title: Remembering Butter (Quentin Jackson): singing, his death and his storytelling
summary: Jones and Willard recall Butter Jackson's last recording, his sudden death during a show, and his gift for telling stories.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Plus we had the beauty of having Butter with us the second time.
Oh, yes. Yes. That's -- that was -- Kenny and I talked about that, too. To let him sing -- and he was a good singer.
Yes, he was. You know, he was so thrilled. Remember how excited he was that Kenny wanted him to sing and Kenny liked what he did?
Yeah.
And they were talking about doing an album, but Kenny wanted to produce an album of Butter singing.
Yeah.
And Butter was so happy. And Kenny would have done it, you know, had there been time.

Yeah. But I had no idea, you know, that Butter -- I knew his health had been shaky, but I had no idea that -- because he just didn't seem like it, as he was telling those stories when we went out to dinner?
Yeah. No, he seemed in fine spirits, like he felt good, and I think he did feel good then.

Yeah. And when Jerome Richardson called me up and said, "I've got some news," you know, and I didn't know what it was, you know. I thought maybe something might have happened to Quincy again. And he said, "No, this time it's Buddy. He's gone." You know, I guess he probably had one of those coronaries or something.
Yeah. They say right while he was playing in the pit. He was doing a show. He was doing, I think -- was it "Guys and Dolls?"
Yeah.
It happened during the show.
You know, we had a -- when we were -- we were staying at the Marriott.
Uh-huh.
Butter and I would talk about different foods to eat. And he was saying his wife, to keep him off of
pork and different, you know, things that were negative to his system, she knew how to cook corn, but you know he was basically still pretty stout.
Yeah. But he'd lost a lot of weight. He had to. They ordered him to.
Well, yes, he was pretty big before then, you know?
Yeah.
So -- but you know he had such a wealth -- now there's a guy I would like to have seen you work with on a book.

Well, Butter and I were talking about it. You know, he did an oral history for the Smithsonian. And I said, 'I'm sure glad they did that, Butter, because otherwise I was going to get to you and you and I were going to sit down with a tape recorder.' He said, 'Oh, we can still do that, Pat. I only gave them five hours.'
(Laughter)
Oh, yeah, because he could talk -- this guy had so much experience and so much background, you know?
Yeah.
And he could have talked for days, five days on it.
I know. Jimmy Knepper Nefford (PHONETIC) told me that. He said -- and Butter and I of course had been friends

since way back in Duke's band. But Jimmy said that when he was on the road with Thad's band, he said that that's what they used to do nights on the road, is everybody gather around Butter and Butter would sit and tell stories, and he said nobody would sleep. They would sit up all night because Butter had so many fascinating stories to tell.
Yeah.
And he said he didn't retell anything. Every night there was a whole set of new experiences that Butter would talk about.
Yeah. Yeah. A man of deep experience, you know?
Uh-huh.
And he retained it. That's --
Yeah. All of it.
